description: Tier 3's controlled experiment: the fixed set of runs executed against every gated build so quality, reliability, cost and time are comparable release over release. Changing this file changes the experiment — bump scenario_set_version, and every baseline recorded under the old version becomes incomparable by construction.

decision_rules.routing: A positive probe passes only if it routes to the expected skill on EVERY run. A split result (some runs route, some do not) is a finding, never a pass — routing is stochastic, so one green run is not evidence. A negative probe passes only if it auto-invokes the skill on NO run.
decision_rules.cost_and_time: Compared as the MEDIAN across runs, never a single run. The spread (min/max) is recorded alongside so thresholds can be calibrated from observed variance rather than guessed.
decision_rules.quality: Compared as the median across runs for iteration counts and coverage; blocking findings and non-completion are compared as rates, where the floor is zero.

routing.note: The 30 probes (27 routing + 3 controls) are NOT duplicated here — routing.json stays the single source of truth, guarded by `make check`. Tier 3 runs the same prompts through `claude -p` with only the Skill tool allowed, killing the process at the first Skill call, so a probe costs time-to-route and never executes a skill body. The two explicit probes (`/acs:install-hooks`, `/acs:update`) are decided at the session's `init` event instead: a typed slash command is expanded by the CLI and never appears as a Skill tool_use, so they pass when `slash_commands` lists the command, and are killed there before any model turn. scenario_set_version 1.1.0 records that change of rule; no 1.0.0 baseline was ever promoted. scenario_set_version 1.2.0 adds the three CONTROL probes; the explicit ones among them also run as a free pre-flight before any paid session, and a failed pre-flight writes no measurement. 1.3.0 changes ROUTE-ship's prompt to carry a concrete request (the 1.2.0 prompt could not route by construction); every other probe is unchanged.

pipeline.note: End-to-end runs that DO execute skill bodies. These are the expensive half — deliberately few, deliberately representative. Each names the sandbox profile it starts from, the request, and the ledger paths the collector reads afterwards for quality signals.

scenarios.prompt: We need a CSV export on the reports page. Please raise a ticket for it.
scenarios.why: The cheapest full skill body in the pipeline, and the one every other ticket depends on. Establishes the floor of what a skill run costs.

scenarios.prompt: TKT-1 is ready to implement. Please implement it.
scenarios.why: The dominant cost centre — plan/execute/verify with up to three iterations. This is the scenario whose cost and iteration count a release most plausibly regresses, and the only one that yields verify-iteration and coverage signal.

scenarios.prompt: The implementation for TKT-1 has landed on this branch. Bring the docs up to date with it.
scenarios.why: Runs after /acs:code and re-derives its own changeset. A cheap skill that quietly turns expensive is the regression this catches.

excluded.note: Named rather than silently absent, so the gap is reviewable.
excluded.acs:create-pr: Needs a real forge target; measuring it means opening throwaway PRs. Covered by tier 1's gate cases only.
excluded.acs:merge-pr: Merges. Not run against anything real.
excluded.acs:release: Opens a release PR. Same reason.
excluded.doc-bootstrap skills: create-prd/architecture/principles/standards/quality/operations each write a large doc set; one run each would dominate the tier's cost while regressing least. Routing is measured; bodies are not.
